Star Ratings Pod 1, Condition 1: Average Curve and Scale Regions

Author

Jamie C. Lee

Published

October 8, 2026

Summary

  • The average curve rises across the whole scale. A 0.4-star gap feels like 19 points at the bottom (1.0 vs 1.4) and 65 at the top (4.6 vs 5.0), on a 0–100 scale. People do not read the scale as evenly spaced.
  • The clearest boundary is just below 4 stars. Of the three-region models, the version that lets the curve jump at a boundary fits best (lowest BIC in both analyses: “Step, 2 breakpoints (3 regions)” with all pairs, “Step, 2 breakpoints (3 regions)” without the top pair). Its lower boundary is at 3.75, between pairs 3.5 vs 3.9 and 3.6 vs 4.0, where pairs start to reach 4 stars.
  • Region slopes (step version, all 37 pairs).
    • Below the boundary (midpoints 1.2–3.75): rises 7.9 points per star, p < .001.
    • Middle region (3.75–4.35): -5.0 points per star, not different from 0 (p = .383). A 0.4-star gap feels equally large throughout.
    • Top region (4.35–4.8): rises steeply, 44.1 points per star, p < .001.
  • The upper boundary is about the end of the scale. With all pairs, the upper breakpoint lands at the highest point the method allows in most bootstrap samples (77% and 92% for the elbow and step versions). It is tracking the jump at 4.6 vs 5.0, not a boundary inside the scale. Without the top pair (Section 2b), the step version gives the same picture: a boundary at 3.75, a flat middle region (-3.5, p = .985) and a rise near the top.
  • Every whole star acts as a small boundary, most strongly at 4. Pairs that straddle a whole star (e.g. 2.7 vs 3.1) feel larger than their neighbors, by 3.6 points at 2 stars, 1.2 at 3 and 5.9 at 4. The midpoint of the scale (3) is the weakest boundary, and 4 the strongest. That fits a “4 stars = good” cutoff better than a split at the midpoint.
  • What this means for negative / neutral / positive. The data point to one strong boundary near 4 stars plus a separate end-of-scale effect. They do not show two clear boundaries around a neutral middle. Read the slope tests with the caveats in Section 5: the average curve blends people whose boundaries differ, and straight lines cannot represent the whole-star bumps.

Data

Each condition 1 participant rated 37 pairs of star ratings on a 1-to-5 scale. In each pair, Rating B is 0.4 stars above Rating A, and the pairs move up the scale one step at a time: 1.0 vs 1.4, 1.1 vs 1.5, …, 4.6 vs 5.0. For each pair, participants said how large the difference felt on a 0–100 slider. Each pair is placed at its midpoint (Rating A + 0.2), so the 37 pairs sit at 1.2, 1.3, …, 4.8.

Every pair is the same 0.4 stars apart. If people read the scale literally, the curve would be flat; where it rises, pairs in that part of the scale feel more different than their gap.

                 if (use_attention_filter) "Passed the attention-check rule (a0.0 and d_probe_rating both below 10)"
                 else "All condition 1 participants")) |>

1. The average curve

The thick line is the mean response at each pair, with its 95% confidence band. The thin gray lines are individual participants.

Smoothed curve and where it rises

A smooth curve (a generalized additive model, GAM) is fitted through all responses, with a random intercept and slope per participant so that each person’s overall level and tilt are accounted for. The lower panel shows the curve’s slope: how fast perceived difference changes per star at each point. Shaded spans are where the slope’s 95% interval is entirely above 0, so the curve is clearly rising there. These are pointwise intervals, so short isolated spans should be read cautiously.

Show code 
gam_fit <- gam(y ~ s(x, k = 20) + s(id, bs = "re") + s(id, x, bs = "re"),
               data = long, method = "REML")
grid <- tibble(x = seq(min(xs), max(xs), length.out = 400), id = long$id[1])
Xp <- predict(gam_fit, grid, type = "lpmatrix")
keep_cols <- !grepl("s\\(id", colnames(Xp))
b <- coef(gam_fit)
set.seed(seed)
sims <- MASS::mvrnorm(2000, b, vcov(gam_fit))
fits_sim <- Xp[, keep_cols] %*% t(sims[, keep_cols])
h <- diff(grid$x[1:2])
derivs <- (fits_sim[-1, ] - fits_sim[-nrow(fits_sim), ]) / h

gam_curve <- tibble(x = grid$x, fit = drop(Xp[, keep_cols] %*% b[keep_cols]),
                    lo = apply(fits_sim, 1, quantile, .025), hi = apply(fits_sim, 1, quantile, .975))
gam_deriv <- tibble(x = grid$x[-1] - h / 2, d = rowMeans(derivs),
                    lo = apply(derivs, 1, quantile, .025), hi = apply(derivs, 1, quantile, .975)) |>
  mutate(rising = lo > 0)
rise_spans <- gam_deriv |>
  mutate(run = cumsum(rising != lag(rising, default = first(rising)))) |>
  filter(rising) |>
  group_by(run) |>
  summarise(xmin = min(x), xmax = max(x), .groups = "drop")
Show code 
shade <- geom_rect(data = rise_spans, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
                   fill = orange, alpha = 0.12)
p1 <- ggplot() + shade +
  geom_point(data = mean_curve, aes(x, m), color = ink2, size = 1.4) +
  geom_ribbon(data = gam_curve, aes(x, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = blue, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = gam_curve, aes(x, fit), color = blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Perceived difference", title = "Smoothed average curve (dots = raw means)") +
  theme_pod
p2 <- ggplot() + shade +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(data = gam_deriv, aes(x, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = blue, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(data = gam_deriv, aes(x, d), color = blue, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of the rating pair (stars)", y = "Slope (points per star)",
       title = "How fast the curve changes; shaded = clearly rising") +
  theme_pod
p1 / p2

The curve rises in separate spurts rather than smoothly. Each spurt ends near a midpoint where the pair starts to straddle a whole star: 1.8 (1.6 vs 2.0), 2.8 (2.6 vs 3.0), 3.8 (3.6 vs 4.0) and 4.8 (4.6 vs 5.0). Section 3 tests this directly.

2. Three regions: negative, neutral, positive

The model

A “broken-stick” regression fits a straight line within each region, joined at two breakpoints. Two breakpoints give three regions. Labeling them negative, neutral and positive is an interpretation of the result, not something the model knows.

Two versions are fitted:

  • Elbow (continuous): the lines meet at each breakpoint, so the curve only bends.
  • Step (discontinuous): each region gets its own line, so the curve can also jump at a breakpoint. A sharp category boundary would look like a jump.

Finding the breakpoints. Every possible pair of breakpoint locations is tried (each region must contain at least 5 rating pairs), and the pair with the smallest error is kept. Every participant rated the same pairs, so fitting the mean curve gives the same lines as fitting all responses with a separate baseline per person. That makes the search fast enough to repeat 2000 times in the bootstrap.

Testing the slopes. A slope of 0 means a 0.4-star gap feels equally large everywhere in that region. Breakpoints chosen to fit the data make ordinary slope tests too optimistic, so the slopes are tested three ways:

  1. Bootstrap (main test). Participants are re-drawn with replacement 2000 times. Each time, the breakpoints are found again and each region’s slope is re-estimated, so the interval includes the uncertainty about where the regions are. The p-value is twice the share of samples on the other side of 0.
  2. Mixed model. All individual responses at the chosen breakpoints, with each participant allowed their own intercept and region slopes. Its p-values treat the breakpoints as known in advance, so they are somewhat too optimistic.
  3. Split-half. Breakpoints are found in a random half of participants (A) and the slopes are tested only in the other half (B), whose data played no part in choosing the regions.

The analysis is run twice: with all 37 pairs, as requested, and without the top pair (4.6 vs 5.0), which turns out to dominate the upper breakpoint.

2a. All 37 pairs

Show code 
R_all$p_fit

Is three regions the right number? Each model is refitted to all individual responses (random intercept per participant). Lower BIC = better fit after a penalty for extra parameters; differences under about 6 are close to ties. These numbers treat the breakpoints as known, so they flatter every breakpoint model somewhat.

3. Another kind of boundary: crossing a whole star

The table in Section 1 shows a regular pattern. Pairs that straddle a whole star (for example 2.7 vs 3.1, which runs from “two-point-something” to “three-point-something”) are rated higher than the pairs just before and after them. They come in blocks of four (midpoints 1.8–2.1, 2.8–3.1, 3.8–4.1), followed by a drop. That is what a boundary at every whole star would produce: the leading digit acts as a category.

This model adds a straight-line trend plus a separate bump for each whole star crossed. The top pair also crosses 5, but it is also the end of the scale, so the two cannot be separated; it gets its own term. Each participant has their own intercept and overall slope.

Show code 
tibble(Term = c("Overall slope (points per star)", "Crossing 2 stars", "Crossing 3 stars",
                "Crossing 4 stars", "Top pair (crosses 5; scale end)"),
       Estimate = ws_co[c("x", "cross2", "cross3", "cross4", "top"), "Estimate"],
       SE = ws_co[c("x", "cross2", "cross3", "cross4", "top"), "Std. Error"],
       p = ws_co[c("x", "cross2", "cross3", "cross4", "top"), "Pr(>|t|)"]) |>
  mutate(Estimate = sprintf("%.1f", Estimate), SE = sprintf("%.1f", SE), p = fmt_p(p)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrr", caption = "Mixed model: trend plus a bump for each whole star crossed (points on the 0-100 slider)")
Mixed model: trend plus a bump for each whole star crossed (points on the 0-100 slider)
Term Estimate SE p
Overall slope (points per star) 9.9 0.6 < .001
Crossing 2 stars 3.6 0.5 < .001
Crossing 3 stars 1.2 0.5 .015
Crossing 4 stars 5.9 0.5 < .001
Top pair (crosses 5; scale end) 13.6 1.0 < .001
  • Does crossing a whole star matter at all? Adding one shared crossing bump (plus the top-pair term) to a straight line improves the fit: χ²(2) = 257.6, p < .001.
  • Are the three bumps the same size? Letting crossings at 2, 3 and 4 differ, compared with one shared bump: χ²(2) = 47.5, p < .001. A small p means some whole stars act as stronger boundaries than others, which is what a negative/neutral/positive account predicts. Here the crossing into 4 stars is the largest bump and the crossing into 3 the smallest.
Show code 
ws_pred <- long_ws |> distinct(x, cross2, cross3, cross4, top) |> arrange(x)
fe <- lme4::fixef(ws_each)
ws_pred$yhat <- fe["(Intercept)"] + fe["x"] * ws_pred$x + fe["cross2"] * ws_pred$cross2 +
  fe["cross3"] * ws_pred$cross3 + fe["cross4"] * ws_pred$cross4 + fe["top"] * ws_pred$top
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = mean_curve, aes(x, m), color = ink2, size = 1.8) +
  geom_step(data = ws_pred, aes(x, yhat), color = orange, linewidth = 1.1, direction = "mid") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(1.75, 2.75, 3.75), linetype = "dotted", color = ink2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 5, 0.5)) +
  labs(x = "Midpoint of the rating pair (stars)", y = "Mean perceived difference",
       title = "Trend plus whole-star bumps (orange) against the raw means (dots)",
       subtitle = "Dotted lines: first pair in each block that straddles a whole star") +
  theme_pod

How this relates to the three-region analysis: the broken-stick lines cannot represent bumps, so they bend to average over them. The elbow found near 3.4–3.85 sits where the crossing into 4 stars begins and the overall level steps up. The two accounts are not exclusive, and the data here cannot fully separate them.

4. Robustness: all condition 1 participants

The breakpoint search on the mean curve of all 187 condition 1 participants, including the 20 who failed the attention-check rule.

Show code 
long_all <- to_long(raw)
ybar_all <- long_all |> group_by(x) |> summarise(m = mean(y), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(x)
rob <- function(keep, label) {
  xv <- xs[xs %in% keep]
  yb <- matrix(ybar_all$m[ybar_all$x %in% xv], ncol = 1)
  e <- best_fit(xv, yb, 2, "elbow")[[1]]; s <- best_fit(xv, yb, 2, "step")[[1]]
  tibble(Pairs = label, Model = c("Elbow (continuous)", "Step (can jump)"),
         Breakpoints = c(fmt_br(e$br), fmt_br(s$br)),
         `Slopes (regions 1, 2, 3)` = c(paste(sprintf("%.1f", e$slopes), collapse = ", "),
                                        paste(sprintf("%.1f", s$slopes), collapse = ", ")))
}
main_rows <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Pairs = "All 37", Model = c("Elbow (continuous)", "Step (can jump)"),
         Breakpoints = c(fmt_br(R_all$ef$br), fmt_br(R_all$sf$br)),
         `Slopes (regions 1, 2, 3)` = c(paste(sprintf("%.1f", R_all$ef$slopes), collapse = ", "),
                                        paste(sprintf("%.1f", R_all$sf$slopes), collapse = ", "))),
  tibble(Pairs = "Without top pair", Model = c("Elbow (continuous)", "Step (can jump)"),
         Breakpoints = c(fmt_br(R_cut$ef$br), fmt_br(R_cut$sf$br)),
         `Slopes (regions 1, 2, 3)` = c(paste(sprintf("%.1f", R_cut$ef$slopes), collapse = ", "),
                                        paste(sprintf("%.1f", R_cut$sf$slopes), collapse = ", "))))
bind_rows(main_rows |> mutate(Sample = sprintf("Passed checks (n = %d)", n_id)),
          bind_rows(rob(xs, "All 37"), rob(xs[xs < 4.75], "Without top pair")) |>
            mutate(Sample = sprintf("All condition 1 (n = %d)", nrow(raw)))) |>
  select(Sample, everything()) |>
  kable()

5. Caveats

  • The average curve blends people. If participants put their boundaries in different places, averaging smears each person’s sharp step into a gentle slope. An average “elbow” can come from many people’s steps at slightly different points, and a region slope can partly reflect that spread. The individual-level analysis in pod1_analysis.qmd found individual boundaries too noisy to estimate one person at a time.
  • Regions are not labels. The model finds where the curve’s behavior changes. Calling the regions negative, neutral and positive is an interpretation. It would be stronger if the breakpoints lined up with where participants themselves say ratings stop being negative and start being positive.
  • The top pair drives the upper breakpoint. With all 37 pairs, the upper breakpoint lands at the limit set by the minimum region size, so it reflects the scale’s end rather than a boundary inside it. Section 2b is the better guide to the interior of the scale.
  • Straight lines cannot represent the whole-star bumps. Region slopes average over them, so a slope that differs from 0 does not by itself mean perception changes smoothly within the region.
  • Responses are not independent. The bootstrap resamples whole participants, which respects that each person gave 37 related answers. The mixed-model checks treat a person’s responses as independent once their own intercept and slopes are accounted for, which is an approximation.
